title: Medieval Europe: Life & Society in the Middle Ages
description: Life in medieval Europe, c. 1000–1500 — the feudal system, castles, the Church, village and town life, the Black Death, and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

notes.heading: The Feudal System
notes.body: After the Norman Conquest of England in **1066**, William the Conqueror organised society into the **feudal system**, a hierarchy based on land and loyalty. At the top was the **king**, who in theory owned all the land. He granted large estates, called **fiefs**, to his most important followers — **tenants-in-chief** (barons and bishops) — in return for military service and loyalty, sworn in a ceremony of **homage**. The lords in turn granted land to **knights**, who promised to fight for them when required. At the bottom were the **peasants** (about 90% of the population), who farmed small strips of land. Most were **serfs** or villeins: not free to leave their village without their lord's permission, and owing the lord several days of unpaid labour each week on his own land, plus rents and fees. In return, the lord offered protection and the right to farm. The system held society together through a chain of mutual obligations, but it also locked almost everyone into the position they were born into.

notes.heading: Castles and Their Evolution
notes.body: **Castles** were the military and administrative heart of medieval lordship. The earliest Norman castles, built rapidly after 1066, were **motte-and-bailey** designs: a wooden tower on an earth mound (the motte) with a fenced courtyard (the bailey) below. They could be raised in weeks but were vulnerable to fire and rot. From the twelfth century, lords rebuilt in stone: the **keep** (a great stone tower, such as the White Tower in London) gave defence, storage and impressive lordly accommodation. By the thirteenth century, **concentric castles** appeared, with rings of walls one inside another, round towers (harder to undermine than square ones), gatehouses with **portcullises** and **drawbridges**, and **arrow slits** and battlements for defenders. Siege warfare drove these changes: attackers used **siege towers**, **battering rams**, **trebuchets** (giant catapults) and **mining** (tunnelling under walls). By the late Middle Ages, gunpowder artillery made high stone walls obsolete, and castles gradually became comfortable country houses — a change from fortress to status symbol.

notes.heading: The Role of the Church
notes.body: The Christian **Church** touched every part of medieval life. Religion gave shape to the year — saints' days, harvest festivals, Easter and Christmas — and to life itself, through baptism, marriage and burial. The **parish priest** was often the only educated man in a village, and the church building was the community's centre. Every household paid a **tithe**, a tax of one-tenth of its produce or income, to support the Church. Above the parishes stood bishops, cathedrals and, at the summit, the **Pope** in Rome, whose authority could rival kings — when King John of England quarrelled with the Pope, England was placed under an **interdict** (1208–1214), suspending church services across the whole kingdom. **Monasteries** housed monks and nuns who prayed, copied manuscripts, ran schools and hospitals, and sheltered travellers — preserving learning through the early medieval centuries. The Church taught that good Christians went to heaven and sinners to hell, so religion offered comfort and meaning, but also gave the Church enormous power over people's minds and money.

notes.heading: Village Life and the Manor
notes.body: Most medieval people lived and died in farming villages organised as **manors** — the lord's estate. At the centre stood the **manor house**, church and mill; around them lay the village cottages and the great open fields, farmed in strips under the **three-field system**, which rotated crops (wheat, then oats or beans, then fallow) to keep the soil fertile. Peasant life was hard and repetitive: ploughing, sowing, weeding and harvesting by season, with women also brewing, baking, spinning and raising children. Homes were small timber-and-**wattle-and-daub** cottages with thatched roofs and smoky central hearths, often shared with animals. Diets were plain — bread, pottage (a thick vegetable stew), cheese and ale — and famine was a real threat when harvests failed. Justice came through the **manor court**, which fined villagers for offences from brawling to letting pigs stray. Yet village life had its pleasures: holy days (holidays), feasts, dancing, and games. For most peasants, the village was the whole world; many never travelled more than a day's walk from home.

notes.heading: Towns, Guilds and Trade
notes.body: From about 1100, towns grew rapidly across Europe as trade revived. Towns such as London, York, Bruges and Venice became centres of **commerce** and crafts. Their wealth came from markets, fairs and long-distance trade in wool, cloth, wine, salt and spices. Craftsmen organised themselves into **guilds** — associations of bakers, weavers, smiths or shoemakers that controlled who could practise a trade, set quality standards and prices, trained **apprentices** (who lived with a master for years learning the craft, then became **journeymen** and eventually masters), and supported members in sickness or old age. Town air was said to make people free: a serf who lived in a town for a year and a day could legally claim freedom from his lord. But towns were crowded, dirty and dangerous — narrow streets, open sewers and timber houses packed together meant disease and fire spread fast. Rich **merchants** dominated town governments, building fine houses and churches, while labourers, beggars and criminals crowded the poorer districts. Even so, towns offered opportunity that the countryside never could.

notes.heading: The Black Death
notes.body: In **1347–1351**, Europe was struck by the **Black Death**, the deadliest pandemic in recorded history. The disease — **bubonic plague**, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis — travelled along trade routes from Asia, carried by fleas living on black rats, and reached England in 1348. Victims developed fever and black swellings (buboes) in the groin and armpits; most died within days. Contemporaries had no understanding of germs: they blamed bad air (**miasma**), divine punishment, or poisoned wells, and responses ranged from prayer and flagellation to, horrifically, attacks on Jewish communities scapegoated for the plague. Between one-third and one-half of Europe's population died — in England perhaps two million people. The consequences transformed society: with labour suddenly scarce, surviving peasants could demand higher wages and refuse feudal duties; whole villages were abandoned; and the authority of lords and the Church was shaken. The plague returned repeatedly for centuries, but the first great outbreak marks a turning point in the slow collapse of feudalism.

notes.heading: The Peasants' Revolt, 1381
notes.body: In the summer of **1381**, thousands of English peasants rose in the largest popular revolt of the Middle Ages. Its causes were layered: after the Black Death, workers wanted freedom and better wages, but the government had passed the **Statute of Labourers** (1351) to freeze wages at pre-plague levels; feudal dues still burdened serfs; and to pay for the failing war with France, Parliament imposed a series of **poll taxes** — flat taxes on every adult, which hit the poor hardest. When tax collectors tried to force payment in Essex and Kent, villages rose up. Led by **Wat Tyler**, the rebels marched on London, burning tax records and the palace of the king's uncle, John of Gaunt. The fourteen-year-old **King Richard II** met the rebels at Mile End and Smithfield, promising an end to serfdom. Tyler was killed at Smithfield, the rebels were dispersed, and Richard broke his promises — hundreds were executed. Yet the revolt was not a total failure: no more poll taxes were levied, and serfdom faded away over the following century as landlords quietly commuted labour services for cash rents.

flashcards.definition: The medieval hierarchy of land and loyalty: the king granted land to lords, lords to knights, and peasants worked the land in return for protection.
flashcards.example: In England after 1066, William I granted fiefs to his barons, who owed him knights' military service.

flashcards.definition: An unfree peasant bound to a lord's manor, owing labour service and rents, and unable to leave the village without permission.
flashcards.example: A serf might owe his lord three days' work each week on the lord's own fields before farming his own strip.

flashcards.definition: The early Norman castle design: a wooden tower on an earth mound (motte) with a fenced courtyard (bailey) — fast to build but vulnerable to fire.
flashcards.example: Hundreds of motte-and-bailey castles were thrown up across England in the years after 1066.

flashcards.definition: The great stone tower at the heart of a later medieval castle, serving as strongpoint, storehouse and lordly residence.
flashcards.example: The White Tower at the Tower of London, begun by William the Conqueror, is a Norman keep.

flashcards.definition: A tax of one-tenth of a household's produce or income, paid to support the medieval Church.
flashcards.example: A peasant family gave every tenth sack of grain from the harvest to the parish church.

flashcards.definition: A religious community of monks or nuns who prayed, copied manuscripts, and ran schools, hospitals and shelters for travellers.
flashcards.example: Monks at a monastery preserved classical learning by hand-copying ancient manuscripts.

flashcards.definition: The lord's estate: the manor house, church, mill, village and surrounding fields farmed by peasant tenants.
flashcards.example: The manor court fined villagers for offences and settled disputes over land.

flashcards.definition: The medieval crop rotation in which open fields were divided into three parts — one with a winter crop, one with a spring crop, one left fallow to recover.
flashcards.example: A village planted wheat in one field, beans in the second, and let animals graze the resting third field.

flashcards.definition: An association of craftsmen or merchants in a town that controlled training, quality and prices, and supported its members.
flashcards.example: The weavers' guild set standards for cloth and trained apprentices to become journeymen and masters.

flashcards.definition: The bubonic plague pandemic of 1347–1351, spread by fleas on rats along trade routes, which killed a third to a half of Europe's population.
flashcards.example: The plague reached England in 1348 and killed perhaps two million people in three years.

flashcards.definition: A flat-rate tax charged on every adult, regardless of wealth — the immediate trigger of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381.
flashcards.example: Three poll taxes to fund the war with France pushed Essex and Kent villagers into rebellion.

flashcards.definition: Leader of the Kentish rebels in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381; killed at Smithfield while negotiating with King Richard II.
flashcards.example: After Tyler's death, Richard II dispersed the rebels and later revoked his promises to end serfdom.

questions.stem: In the feudal system, who stood at the top of the hierarchy and in theory owned all the land?
choices: The Pope
The king
The richest merchant
The knights
questions.explanation: The king was at the apex of feudal society. He granted land (fiefs) to his tenants-in-chief in return for loyalty and military service, and all other grants of land flowed down from him.

questions.stem: What did peasants owe their lord under the feudal system?
choices: Nothing — peasants owned their land outright
Military service as knights in the lord's army
Several days of unpaid labour each week on the lord's land, plus rents and fees
A tenth of their income to the lord instead of the Church
questions.explanation: Peasants, especially serfs, owed labour service on the lord's demesne as well as rents and manorial fees. The tithe (a tenth) went to the Church, not the lord, and military service was the knight's obligation.

questions.stem: The earliest Norman castles, built quickly after 1066, were:
choices: Concentric stone castles with rings of walls
Motte-and-bailey castles of timber and earth
Brick palaces with large windows
Iron fortresses built by cannon foundries
questions.explanation: The Normans needed fortifications fast, and motte-and-bailey castles — a wooden tower on an earth mound with a fenced courtyard — could be raised in weeks. Stone keeps and concentric designs came later.

questions.stem: Why did medieval lords increasingly rebuild their castles in stone from the twelfth century onwards?
choices: Stone was cheaper and quicker to build with than timber
Timber castles caught fire easily and rotted, while stone resisted fire, siege engines and mining
The Church required all castles to be made of stone
Gunpowder made wooden castles too powerful
questions.explanation: Wooden towers burned and decayed. Stone keeps and curtain walls withstood fire, battering and undermining far better, and also displayed the lord's wealth and power. Stone was much more expensive and slower to build, which is why the change was gradual.

questions.stem: Which of these best shows the power of the medieval Church over ordinary people's lives?
choices: The Church had no role outside Sunday services
Only monks and nuns paid any attention to religion
The Church ran the feudal system on behalf of the king
Everyone paid the tithe, the Church controlled baptism, marriage and burial, and belief in heaven and hell shaped daily behaviour
questions.explanation: The Church touched everyone: it taxed all households through the tithe, marked every stage of life with sacraments, ran schools and hospitals, and its teachings about the afterlife gave it authority over minds as well as money.

choices: A tax of one-tenth of produce or income paid to the Church
A fine imposed by the manor court
A coin used to pay knights
A tenth of a knight's land
questions.explanation: The tithe was the Church's tax — one-tenth of everything a household produced or earned. It was widely resented, especially by the poor, because everyone paid the same proportion.

questions.stem: What was the main purpose of a craft guild in a medieval town?
choices: To organise crusades to the Holy Land
To collect the poll tax for the king
To run the local monastery
To control who could practise a trade, maintain quality and prices, and train apprentices
questions.explanation: Guilds regulated their craft: only guild members could trade, apprentices were trained over years to become journeymen and masters, and the guild enforced quality standards and supported members in hardship.

questions.stem: The Black Death of 1347–1351 was spread mainly by:
choices: Poisoned wells in the cities
Fleas living on rats, travelling along trade routes
Bad air rising from swamps
Soldiers returning from the crusades
questions.explanation: Bubonic plague is caused by a bacterium carried by fleas that lived on black rats. The rats moved along trade routes in ships and carts, carrying the disease from Asia to Europe. Contemporaries blamed miasma or poisoned wells because they did not know about germs.

questions.stem: Why did the Black Death strengthen the position of peasants who survived it?
choices: The king freed all serfs immediately in 1348
The Church gave peasants free land as charity
With up to half the population dead, labour was scarce, so surviving workers could demand higher wages and refuse feudal duties
Peasants inherited the castles of dead lords
questions.explanation: Mass death created a severe labour shortage. Lords competed for workers, so surviving peasants bargained for wages and freedom their grandparents could never have imagined — a key long-term consequence that undermined serfdom.

questions.stem: What was the immediate trigger of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
choices: The outbreak of the Black Death
Attempts to collect a new poll tax that fell on every adult
The Norman Conquest
A bad harvest and famine
questions.explanation: The revolt began in Essex and Kent when collectors tried to enforce the third poll tax — a flat tax on every adult that hit the poor hardest. Deeper causes included the Statute of Labourers and resentment of serfdom, but the poll tax sparked the rising.

questions.stem: Who led the Kentish rebels during the Peasants' Revolt, and what happened to him?
choices: Wat Tyler — killed at Smithfield while negotiating with Richard II
John Ball — crowned king by the rebels
Richard II — executed by the peasants
John of Gaunt — driven into exile in France
questions.explanation: Wat Tyler led the Kentish rebels into London and met the young King Richard II at Smithfield, where he was killed during the negotiations. John Ball was a radical priest involved in the revolt, but Tyler was its military leader.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the outcome of the Peasants' Revolt?
choices: The rebels overthrew the king and ended feudalism at once
The revolt was crushed and its promises revoked, yet no more poll taxes were levied and serfdom gradually faded away over the next century
The rebels won higher wages that were guaranteed by law forever
Nothing changed in any way after 1381
questions.explanation: In the short term the revolt failed — Tyler was dead, Richard II broke his promises and rebels were executed. But in the long term the poll tax was abandoned and landlords increasingly replaced labour services with cash rents, so serfdom withered. Revolts can fail yet still have lasting consequences.

questions.stem: Which list shows castle development in the correct chronological order?
choices: Concentric stone castle → motte-and-bailey castle → stone keep
Motte-and-bailey castle → stone keep → concentric castle
Stone keep → motte-and-bailey castle → concentric castle
Concentric castle → stone keep → motte-and-bailey castle
questions.explanation: Timber motte-and-bailey castles came first (from 1066), followed by stone keeps in the twelfth century, then concentric castles with multiple rings of walls in the thirteenth — each design answering new siege tactics.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the Black Death was a turning point in medieval history. Which evidence best supports this view?
choices: The plague changed very little because kings stayed in power
The plague only affected England, not the rest of Europe
The plague killed only the elderly, so working life continued as normal
The huge death toll broke the labour system, raised wages for survivors, weakened feudal obligations and shook the authority of lords and Church
questions.explanation: A turning point is a moment after which life is measurably different. The plague's mortality transformed the labour market and social relations across the whole of Europe — deep, lasting change affecting millions — which is exactly what makes it significant.

questions.stem: Why did medieval people say "town air makes you free"?
choices: Towns had cleaner air than the countryside
A serf who lived in a town for a year and a day could legally claim freedom from his lord
Town dwellers did not have to pay any taxes
Only free people were allowed to breathe in towns
questions.explanation: Towns stood partly outside the manorial system: custom held that a runaway serf who lived in a town for a year and a day without being claimed became legally free. This made towns magnets for ambitious peasants.
